W2. Philosophy of AI

Author

Munir Makhmutov

Published

September 10, 2026

1. Theory

1.1 Epistemology and the Definition of Knowledge

Epistemology is the branch of philosophy concerned with the nature, sources, and limits of knowledge—derived from the Greek epistēmē (ἐπιστήμη, “knowledge”) and logos (λόγος, “logical discourse” or “study”). It asks the foundational question: how do we know what we know?

In classical philosophy, the standard analytical framework traced to Socrates defines knowledge through the tripartite definition, commonly abbreviated as Justified True Belief (JTB). Under this formulation, a cognitive agent or subject possesses knowledge of a proposition () if and only if three distinct conditions are satisfied simultaneously:

  1. Truth: The proposition corresponds to objective reality. Truth is independent of an observer’s internal state: if is objectively false, it cannot be known.
  2. Belief: The subject accepts as true; it represents the subjective mental representation or internal stance toward reality. One cannot know a fact without believing it.
  3. Justification: The subject possesses an adequate rational explanation, evidence, or epistemic grounding supporting . A mere arbitrary guess that happens to be right does not qualify.

Formally:

  • Why it matters: Artificial intelligence systems—from symbolic knowledge bases and theorem provers to modern neural models—manipulate representations of the world. To assess whether an artificial system truly possesses “knowledge” rather than superficial pattern matching or statistical guessing, we require a formal benchmark separating mere stored data or lucky predictions from epistemically grounded representations.
1.1.1 The Gettier Problem: Accidental Truth

For centuries, JTB was regarded as providing the necessary and sufficient conditions for knowledge. In 1963, American philosopher Edmund Gettier published a landmark paper demonstrating that JTB is insufficient: an agent can hold a justified belief that happens to be true entirely by luck or accident, without possessing genuine knowledge.

  • The Smith and Jones Thought Experiment (Gettier, 1963):
    1. Two applicants, Smith and Jones, apply for a job.
    2. Smith has strong evidence for two premises: the company director assured him that Jones would be chosen, and Smith personally counted 10 coins in Jones’s pocket moments earlier.
    3. From these premises, Smith logically deduces the proposition : “The man who will get the job has 10 coins in his pocket.”
    4. Smith accepts (Belief), and his belief is supported by reliable testimony and direct count (Justification).
    5. In an unexpected reversal, the director hires Smith instead of Jones. Furthermore, entirely unknown to Smith, Smith himself happens to carry exactly 10 coins in his own pocket.
  • Analysis: Proposition is objectively true (Truth); Smith explicitly believes (Belief); and Smith arrived at via valid deduction from credible evidence (Justification). However, Smith clearly did not know —the proposition was made true by a state of affairs (Smith’s coins and Smith’s hiring) completely disconnected from the justification he relied upon (Jones’s coins and Jones’s hiring). His justification proceeded via a justified false belief.
  • The Epistemological Lesson: Justification must be non-accidentally and properly connected to the truth. In AI, this distinction is critical: a predictive model may produce a correct output from an unsound intermediate feature or spurious correlation; while the output is true and nominally justified by its training loss, the system lacks grounded epistemic knowledge.
  • Key Pitfalls:
    • Confusing belief with knowledge: High certainty or probabilistic model confidence is purely subjective; confidence alone never converts an ungrounded or false statement into knowledge.
    • Assuming justification implies truth: An agent can be completely rational, methodologically sound, and fully justified in believing a falsehood (as Smith was regarding Jones’s hiring).
    • Treating JTB as sufficient: Accidental alignment between evidence and reality satisfies JTB mechanically while failing the requirement of genuine epistemic grounding.
1.2 The Turing Test and Operational Intelligence

The Turing Test is an operational definition of machine intelligence proposed by British mathematician Alan Mathison Turing in his seminal 1950 Mind paper, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence.” Instead of debating the subjective, metaphysical question “Can machines think?”, Turing reformulated the inquiry into an empirical criterion of behavioral indistinguishability: can a digital computer successfully imitate human verbal behavior under blind testing conditions?

+------------------+         Teletype Link A         +-------------------+
|                  | <=============================> | Hidden Entity A   |
| Human            |                                 | (Human or Machine)|
| Interrogator (C) |         Teletype Link B         +-------------------+
|                  | <=============================> | Hidden Entity B   |
+------------------+                                 | (Machine or Human)|
                                                     +-------------------+
1.2.1 Turing’s Contributions and Historical Context

Turing’s formulation of operational intelligence built upon foundational milestones in mathematical logic and computing:

  • Universal Turing Machine (UTM) and the Church–Turing Thesis: Formulated during his fellowship at King’s College, Cambridge, proving that a simple abstract machine manipulating discrete symbols on an infinite tape can simulate any algorithmic computation. Turing later completed his PhD at Princeton, declining John von Neumann’s postdoctoral offer to return to Cambridge.
  • Cryptanalysis at Bletchley Park: During World War II, Turing designed the electromechanical Bombe decoder to break the German Enigma cipher. His technical monographs (The Applications of Probability to Cryptography and Paper on Statistics of Repetitions) remained classified by the British government for roughly 70 years.
  • Persecution and Legacy: Despite pioneering artificial intelligence, computer design, and mathematical biology, Turing was criminally prosecuted for homosexuality by the UK government in 1952, leading to chemical castration. He died of cyanide poisoning in 1954. He received an official government apology in 2009 and a royal pardon in 2013.
1.2.2 The Imitation Game Protocol

Turing framed the benchmark as the Imitation Game: 1. Setup: Three participants are isolated in separate rooms: a human interrogator (), a hidden human (), and a hidden machine () running an automated agent. 2. Channel: Communication occurs solely via neutral text interfaces (originally a teletype, avoiding clues from vocal tone, physical appearance, or sensory capabilities). 3. Objective: Interrogator submits arbitrary questions to both entities. Entity (the machine) attempts to deceive into believing it is the human, while entity attempts to assist in making the correct identification. 4. Decision Metric: Let be the probability that interrogator misidentifies the machine as the human. If when testing the machine is statistically comparable to the rate at which an interrogator misidentifies a human playing against another human, the machine has passed the test.

1.2.3 Domain Limitations and Operationalism

The standard Turing Test operates as an external behavioral test: it evaluates input-output functional equivalence rather than underlying cognitive architecture or conscious awareness. * Narrow vs. Broad Domains: While early systems achieved conversational mimicry in restricted domains or through scripted evasions, open-ended conversational coherence across arbitrary common-sense reasoning, humor, and episodic context remains an elusive benchmark for general intelligence. * Asymmetric Competence: The test penalizes machines for super-human capabilities. A system that instantly calculates reveals its artificial identity unless it deliberately delays its response or injects arithmetic errors to simulate human cognitive latency.

1.2.4 The Inverse Turing Test: CAPTCHA

When the roles of the interrogator and respondent are reversed such that an automated system interrogates an unseen user, the protocol becomes an Inverse Turing Test. This is implemented globally as CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart). * Purpose: Provides a computationally cheap, cost-effective defense against automated bots in web workflows: preventing spam in account creation, securing online ordering queues, and protecting email registrations. * Modalities: 1. Distorted Text and OCR: Systems such as early reCAPTCHA presented pairs of distorted character strings (e.g., "Mills," alongside scanned book snippets "sposcz"). The system leveraged human perceptual processing to decipher optical character recognition (OCR) failures encountered during the digitization of physical archives. 2. Image-Grid Classification: Challenges presenting a visual array requiring the user to select all cells containing specific target objects (e.g., “Select all squares with traffic lights”). 3. Audio Challenges: Phonetically distorted spoken words overlaid with ambient noise, serving as accessibility alternatives while resisting automated speech-to-text parsers.

1.2.5 Worked Mini-Illustration: Evaluating an Interrogation Transcript

An interrogator submits a compound prompt over a teletype link:

  • Candidate Machine Model 1 (Raw Compute Engine):
    • Response: "52321. Liquid cellulose interaction causes hydrogen bond degradation."
    • Interrogator Decision: Instantly flagged as machine. Response latency was with immediate exact arithmetic and mechanical prose.
  • Candidate Machine Model 2 (Turing Imitation Strategy):
    • Response (delivered after a pause): "That's around 52,000—52,321 if my mental math holds. As for coffee, the paper fibers soak up the water and swell, and the brown pigments stay behind when it dries, leaving it warped and stained."
    • Interrogator Decision: Indistinguishable from an educated human respondent. The system successfully simulated human response pacing, approximation, and pragmatic discourse.
1.2.6 Common Pitfalls
  • Conflating Operational Indistinguishability with Consciousness: The Turing Test determines whether a system can replicate the external linguistic performance of a human. It does not measure internal semantic understanding, subjective experience (qualia), or sentience. Passing the test satisfies operational behavioral criteria, not philosophical proof of a mind.
  • Confusing Standard Turing Tests with CAPTCHA Directionality: In Turing’s original Imitation Game, a human interrogator evaluates an unknown entity to detect a machine. In a CAPTCHA, a machine algorithm automatically interrogates an unknown remote client to detect whether it is a human.
1.3 Syntax, Semantics, and the Chinese Room Argument

The distinction between syntactic manipulation and semantic comprehension forms the primary philosophical boundary between simulation and true cognition in artificial intelligence. Syntax refers to the formal, structural rules governing the arrangement, combination, and transformation of symbols without regard to their interpretation. Semantics refers to the meaning, reference, truth conditions, and intentionality underlying those symbols—connecting representations to the actual objects, relations, and concepts they denote. Strong AI posits that an appropriately programmed computer does not merely simulate a mind, but literally possesses a mind, consciousness, and genuine understanding. In contrast, Weak AI claims only that computational models are powerful tools for studying cognition and automating intelligent tasks.

       Input (Chinese Characters)
                 │
                 ▼ [In Slot]
       ┌───────────────────────────┐
       │   The Chinese Room        │
       │  ┌─────────────────────┐  │
       │  │ English Speaker     │  │
       │  │ (No Chinese)        │  │
       │  └──────────┬──────────┘  │
       │             │ consults    │
       │  ┌──────────▼──────────┐  │
       │  │ Formal Rulebook     │  │
       │  │ (If "漢" then "語") │  │
       │  └─────────────────────┘  │
       └─────────┬─────────────────┘
                 ▼ [Out Slot]
      Output (Chinese Characters)
1.3.1 The Thought Experiment and the Critique of Strong AI

In 1980, philosopher John Searle introduced the Chinese Room argument to demonstrate that passing an operational assessment such as the Turing Test does not imply genuine mental states or semantic understanding.

The setup is defined as follows: 1. An English-speaking human agent who understands zero Chinese is locked inside an isolated room. 2. Batches of Chinese characters are fed into the room through an in slot. 3. The room contains a comprehensive rulebook written entirely in English. The book provides purely formal instructions: when a specific sequence of symbols is matched, look up the corresponding rule and produce another sequence of characters. 4. The agent executes these lookups, writes the resulting characters onto paper, and passes them out through an out slot.

To an external native Chinese speaker, the room responds fluently and coherently, effortlessly passing an imitation game. Yet, the human inside does not understand a single word of Chinese; they are executing formal symbol manipulations based strictly on shape and syntax. Searle argues that digital computers operate identically: a central processor manipulates bits according to program instructions (syntax) without any intrinsic grasp of what those bits represent (semantics). Therefore, syntax does not suffice for semantics, and behavioural equivalence does not entail intentionality or comprehension.

1.3.2 Counterarguments and Computational Responses

Searle’s thought experiment prompted several key rebuttals:

  • The Systems Reply: While the individual human clerk does not understand Chinese, the entire system—comprising the human, the rulebook, the scratch paper, and the input/output protocol—does instantiate understanding. Cognition is an emergent property of the distributed architecture, much like an individual biological neuron does not understand language, but the human brain as a whole does.
  • External Grounding (The Robot Reply): If the rulebook and processor are placed inside a physical robot equipped with sensors (cameras, microphones) and actuators (manipulators, wheels), the internal symbols become causally linked to physical reality. This interaction grounds abstract syntax in real-world perceptual experience.
  • Rule Induction and Machine Learning: Searle assumed a static, manually hard-coded rulebook written by an external designer (“Who writes the rulebook?”). Modern AI architectures derive and optimize their own latent representations directly from raw data via continuous mathematical optimization, complicating the view that machines are merely static lookup tables.
1.3.3 The Computer Perception Pipeline vs. Conceptualization

The semantic gap is evident in how machine vision bridges low-level sensory signals and high-level human categories. Processing an object follows a four-stage cognitive pipeline:

  1. Segmentation: Partitioning raw digital images into distinct pixel masks corresponding to continuous surfaces or objects.
  2. Detection: Localizing candidate objects within coordinate bounding boxes and assigning probability scores across candidate labels.
  3. Conceptualization: Mapping perceptual features into an invariant functional schema.
  4. Verbalization: Emitting linguistic tokens that denote the classified concept to external agents.

Mini-Illustration: Consider the concept of a chair. In human semantics, a chair is conceptually defined by its functional affordance: “a piece of furniture designed to support a seated human.” Visually, the category spans radical morphological variations:

  • A classical upholstered dark grey armchair with wooden legs;
  • A minimalist slatted wooden upright dining chair;
  • A plush, bright orange children’s armchair shaped like a cartoon tiger;
  • A modern chrome-stemmed height-adjustable swivel bar stool.

A standard object detector treats these instances as distinct pixel distributions, running mathematical filters across arrays to match syntax (edges, textures, spatial convolutions). If the model labels all four as chair, it does so by associating statistical patterns with a character string, not by understanding rest, seating, or bodily posture.

  • Key Pitfall: Do not confuse internal functional correctness with semantic comprehension. An AI system that generates grammatically flawless and contextually accurate replies is manipulating high-dimensional representations according to statistical and formal constraints; this operational competence does not settle whether the machine possesses intentionality or subjective awareness.
1.4 Robot Ethics and Asimov’s Laws

Normative robot ethics formalizes the moral, legal, and operational constraints governing autonomous physical agents. Isaac Asimov originally structured machine morality around the Three Laws of Robotics, organized as a strict lexicographic priority hierarchy: 1. First Law (Non-maleficence): A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm. 2. Second Law (Obedience): A robot must obey the orders given to it by human beings, except where such orders would conflict with the First Law. 3. Third Law (Self-preservation): A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.

To address existential and collective dilemmas, Asimov later introduced the Zeroth Law:

  • Zeroth Law (Collective preservation): A robot may not injure humanity, or, through inaction, allow humanity to come to harm.

The Zeroth Law precedes the First Law, modifying it to: “A robot may not injure a human being, unless this conflicts with the Zeroth Law.” This elevation shifts the framework from deontological, individual-level rights to a utilitarian ethical calculus, requiring an agent to weigh individual harm against aggregate existential risk to the human species.

       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │                      Zeroth Law                        │
       │     Preserve Humanity (Utilitarian macro-calculus)     │
       └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                   │ overrides
       ┌───────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────┐
       │                       First Law                        │
       │       Do Not Harm Individual Humans (Deontological)    │
       └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                   │ overrides
       ┌───────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────┐
       │                      Second Law                        │
       │            Obey Human Orders (Subservience)            │
       └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                   │ overrides
       ┌───────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────┘
       │                       Third Law                        │
       │          Preserve Own Existence (Self-defense)         │
       └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Why it matters: Asimov’s laws expose the limits of high-level rule-based morality. In practice, robots cannot rely on vague natural-language directives (“harm”, “humanity”) without rigorous mathematical definitions of cost, utility, and uncertainty. Modern roboticists separate ethical governance into physical hardware safety envelopes for industry and legal-normative frameworks for lethal tactical systems.
1.4.1 Industrial and Collaborative Physical Safety

Traditional factory robotics guarantees the First Law not through reasoning algorithms, but through deterministic spatial isolation:

  • Industrial caged cells: Heavy high-speed manipulators operate behind rigid metal enclosures. Mechanical interlocks cut actuator power immediately if an access gate opens.
  • Safety mats: Pressure-sensitive floor mats placed in human access zones (Zone 1, Zone 2) register worker weight and trigger emergency stops before the manipulator can sweep through the sector.
  • Light curtains and muting sensors: Optical light curtains project arrays of infrared beams across open workstation boundaries; breaking any beam interrupts the safety circuit. Muting sensors temporarily suppress this trip condition only when an expected, identifiable object (such as a pallet on a conveyor) crosses the boundary, distinguishing materials from humans.
  • Collaborative robots (cobots): Modern systems (such as the dual-armed Rethink Robotics Baxter) replace strict physical isolation with power-and-force limiting, rounded compliant joints, integrated torque sensors, and dynamic vision systems that continuously adjust speed and separation margins when humans enter their shared workspace.
1.4.2 Tactical, Police, and Military Autonomous Systems

When robots operate outside factory cages, legal and operational doctrines replace fictional constraints:

  • Semi-autonomous combat drones: Military uninhabited aerial vehicles (UAVs) conduct surveillance and deliver precision-guided munitions (e.g., Hellfire missiles). Under international humanitarian law (specifically the Geneva Conventions and the Law of Armed Conflict), targeting decisions require distinction, proportionality, and military necessity, typically mediated via human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop command architectures.
  • Municipal tactical robotics: Civil law enforcement operates under constitutional use-of-force standards (e.g., the Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness standard in the US). In the 2016 Dallas police standoff, authorities strapped an explosive payload (detonation cord with C4) to the manipulator arm of an existing Remotec Andros F6A bomb-disposal robot to neutralize an active sniper who had killed five police officers and was barricaded behind cover. This marked the first documented lethal deployment of a domestic police robot in US history, illustrating how human commanders treat robotic platforms as remotely operated lethal tools rather than autonomous moral agents.
1.4.3 Worked Mini-Illustration: Lexicographic Priority vs. Utilitarian Calculus

Consider an autonomous perimeter rover evaluating three available actions :

Action Impact on Human A Impact on Humanity Human Order Compliance Robot Integrity
Harmed () Threat neutralized () Disobeys order () Intact ()
Unharmed () Threat detonates () Obeys order () Intact ()
Unharmed () Threat neutralized () Disobeys order () Destroyed ()
  1. Under the Strict Three Laws (No Zeroth Law):
    • Actions must satisfy first. Action violates Law 1 and is rejected.
    • Between and , both satisfy Law 1 (). Law 2 requires obedience (). Action is selected, even though it results in catastrophic collective harm ().
  2. Under the Zeroth Law Hierarchy:
    • Maximize first. Action is eliminated ().
    • Between and , both achieve . Applying Law 1 eliminates because .
    • Applying Law 3 to permits the robot to sacrifice itself () because protecting its existence is strictly subordinate to Law 1 and the Zeroth Law. Action is executed.
  • Key Pitfalls:
    • Literary trope vs. engineering architecture: Asimov designed the Three Laws deliberately to fail in complex situations, demonstrating that natural language cannot resolve semantic boundary conflicts (e.g., what constitutes “inaction” or psychological “harm”). Engineers do not program Asimov’s laws; they program objective loss functions, deterministic state machines, and hardware fail-safes.
    • Zeroth Law paternalism: The Zeroth Law transforms an agent into a utilitarian maximizer. Because “humanity” is an abstraction, an autonomous system guided purely by aggregate species utility can justify harm, surveillance, or subjugation of individual humans whenever its internal model predicts a net positive macro-outcome.
1.5 Propositional Logic: Propositions, Connectives, and Truth Tables

A proposition is a declarative statement that evaluates to strictly one truth value: either True ( or ) or False ( or ) in classical bivalent logic, but never both simultaneously. A statement that can be assigned a truth value is called an atomic proposition (or propositional variable, typically denoted by lowercase Roman letters ).

Expressions that fail this criterion are not propositions:

  • Imperative commands: Statements that instruct action rather than declare fact (e.g., “Open the window.”).
  • Interrogatives: Inquiries seeking information (e.g., “Is the server running?”).
  • Open expressions with free variables: Statements containing unbound variables whose truth value cannot be determined in isolation without contextual binding or values (e.g., “x + 3 = 5”).

A false statement (e.g., “7 is an even number”) is still a valid proposition because its truth value is definitively .

  • Why it matters: Symbolic logic provides AI systems with an unambiguous mathematical language for knowledge representation, automated theorem proving, and deterministic decision-making, stripping away natural language ambiguities.
1.5.1 Logical Connectives and Truth Conditions

Compound propositions are constructed by joining atomic propositions using formal logical connectives (operators):

  1. Negation (, “NOT ”): A unary operator that inverts the truth value of its operand. is if is , and if is .
  2. Conjunction (, “ AND ”): A binary operator that evaluates to if and only if both and are ; otherwise, it is .
  3. Disjunction (, “ OR ”): The standard logical OR is inclusive disjunction. evaluates to if at least one operand is , evaluating to only when both and are .
  4. Exclusive Disjunction (, “XOR”): Evaluates to if strictly one operand is and the other is . When both operands share identical truth values ( or ), evaluates to .
  5. Conditional (, “Material Implication”): Interpreted as “if , then ”. Here, is the antecedent (hypothesis) and is the consequent (conclusion). The conditional is defined as false in exactly one scenario: when the antecedent is and the consequent is . If is , the implication is automatically regardless of the truth value of —a property known as vacuous truth.
    • “ if ” translates to .
    • “ only if ” translates to .
  6. Biconditional (, “Equivalence” or “IFF”): Interpreted as “p if and only if q”. Evaluates to if and only if both and share the identical truth value (both or both ).

1.5.2 Systematic Truth Table Construction

A truth assignment (interpretation) maps every propositional variable to a specific element of . For a compound formula comprising distinct propositional variables, the systematic truth table requires exactly distinct rows to cover all combinations of truth assignments.

1.5.3 Pitfalls and Clarifications
  • Vacuous Truth Confusion: Everyday human conversation often assumes a causal link between and . In formal logic, material implication requires no causal connection. Consider: “If the Moon is made of cheese (), then ().” Because the antecedent is false, the formula evaluates formally to True.
  • “Only If” vs. “If”: In natural language, students frequently reverse the direction of implication. “You enter the lab () if you have an access card ()” means . In contrast, “You enter the lab () only if you have an access card ()” establishes that having a card is a necessary condition for entering, translating to .
  • Inclusive vs. Exclusive Disjunction: In natural language, “or” is frequently used exclusively (e.g., “You can have tea or coffee” implies not both). In mathematical logic, without qualification is strictly inclusive: . The exclusive interpretation must be designated explicitly as .
1.6 Propositional Reasoning: Equivalences, Conditional Forms, and Satisfiability

A formula’s semantic status depends on how its truth value behaves across the space of all possible truth assignments (models). Propositional reasoning formalizes this behavior to establish semantic validity, test satisfiability, and verify equivalence algebraically without exhaustively calculating rows in truth tables.

1.6.1 Semantic Classification and Satisfiability

Every well-formed propositional formula falls into one of three semantic categories:

  • A tautology is a formula that evaluates to true under every possible truth assignment. Formally, for a formula , for all models (written ). A minimal example is the law of excluded middle: .
  • A contradiction (or unsatisfiable formula) is a formula that evaluates to false under every possible truth assignment. Formally, for every model . A minimal example is .
  • A contingency is a formula that evaluates to true under at least one truth assignment and false under at least one other (e.g., , which is true when both atoms are true, but false under any assignment setting either atom to false).

Satisfiability characterizes whether a formula has at least one model. A formula is satisfiable if and only if there exists at least one truth assignment under which it evaluates to true.

Automated reasoning and constraint satisfaction in AI often reduce planning and verification problems to propositional satisfiability (SAT): deciding whether an assignment exists that satisfies a conjunction of constraints.

1.6.2 Conditional Transformations

Given a directed implication (where is the hypothesis/antecedent and is the conclusion/consequent), three related conditional statements can be formed:

  • Converse: (swaps antecedent and consequent).
  • Inverse: (negates both antecedent and consequent).
  • Contrapositive: (negates and swaps both).

The conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent:

The converse and inverse are also equivalent to each other (), but they are not logically equivalent to the original conditional .

Illustration: Let denote “a polygon is a square” and denote “a polygon is a rectangle.” * Original (): “If a polygon is a square, then it is a rectangle” (True). * Contrapositive (): “If a polygon is not a rectangle, then it is not a square” (True — identical meaning). * Converse (): “If a polygon is a rectangle, then it is a square” (False — rectangles need not have equal sides). * Inverse (): “If a polygon is not a square, then it is not a rectangle” (False — non-squares can still be rectangles).

1.6.5 Common Pitfalls
  • Confusing Satisfiability with Tautology: A formula is satisfiable if at least one row of its truth table is true; it is a tautology only if every row is true. A contingency is satisfiable, but it is not valid.
  • Converse Error (Affirming the Consequent): Treating as interchangeable with . Only the contrapositive preserves the truth value of a conditional.
  • Negating Conditionals as Conditionals: Translating into (the inverse). An implication fails only when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false; hence , which is a conjunction, not an implication.
1.7 First-Order Logic: Syntax, Ontology, and Components

Propositional logic represents the world using monolithic propositional variables (). Because it treats whole declarative assertions as atomic black boxes, it cannot inspect the internal structure of statements, express properties shared by different entities, or generalize over collections of objects. For example, the valid deduction:

  1. Every student is registered.
  2. Ana is a student.
  3. Therefore, Ana is registered.

cannot be proven in propositional logic; treating each assertion as an atomic symbol yields , which is invalid. First-Order Logic (FOL) (also called predicate logic) resolves this representational bottleneck by introducing an explicit ontology of objects, properties, and relations.

                  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                  │   Domain of Discourse (D)    │
                  │   Objects: Ana, Bob, etc.    │
                  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                 │
         ┌───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
         ▼                                               ▼
┌──────────────────┐                           ┌──────────────────┐
│      TERMS       │                           │     FORMULAS     │
│  (refer to D)    │                           │  (truth values)  │
├──────────────────┤                           ├──────────────────┤
│ • Constants: Ana │                           │ • Atomic:        │
│ • Variables: x   │                           │   Student(Ana)   │
│ • Functions:     │───(pass as arguments)────>│   x = y          │
│   mentorOf(x)    │                           │ • Complex:       │
│                  │                           │   P(x) ∧ Q(x)    │
└──────────────────┘                           └──────────────────┘
1.7.1 Ontological Building Blocks

The semantics of FOL are grounded in a universe of entities and syntactic elements that refer to or make assertions about them:

  • Domain of Discourse (): A non-empty set of concrete or abstract entities under consideration (e.g., people in a university, integers, geographical regions).

  • Constants: Fixed syntactic names that refer to specific, individual objects within . For example, , , and denote specific domain members.

  • Variables: Syntactic placeholders (typically written in lowercase, e.g., ) that range over unspecified objects of .

  • Predicates: Symbols representing properties of individual objects or relationships among multiple objects. An -ary predicate maps an ordered tuple of domain elements to a truth value:

    A unary predicate () expresses an intrinsic property or category membership, such as or . An -ary relation () expresses relationships between objects, such as or .

  • Functions: Symbols denoting mappings from an ordered tuple of domain elements to a single, unique domain element:

    Unlike predicates, functions do not evaluate to truth values; they refer to objects. For instance, designates the unique individual who mentors .

  • Equality (): A built-in binary predicate asserting that two distinct syntactic terms refer to the identical object in (e.g., or ).

1.7.2 Terms versus Formulas

FOL strictly separates expressions that refer to objects from expressions that assert truth:

  • Term: Any syntactic expression that refers to an object in the domain . Formally:
    1. Any constant is a term.
    2. Any variable is a term.
    3. If is an -ary function symbol and are terms, then is a term.
    Examples: , , , and are all terms. A term has no truth value.
  • Atomic Formula (or Atom): The simplest logical expression that evaluates to a truth value ( or ). It is formed either by:
    1. Applying an -ary predicate to terms: .
    2. Equating two terms using the equality predicate: .
    Examples: , , and are atomic formulas.
  • Complex Formula: An expression constructed by joining atomic formulas using propositional connectives () or by enclosing them within quantifiers ().
1.7.3 Variable Binding, Scope, and Sentences

Quantifiers (, ) bind variable occurrences across logical subexpressions:

  • Scope: The syntactic subformula over which a quantifier exerts control. In , the scope of is the formula .
  • Bound Variable: An occurrence of a variable that falls within the scope of a quantifier specifying that variable ( or ).
  • Free Variable: An occurrence of a variable that is not bound by any quantifier in whose scope it lies.
  • Sentence (or Closed Formula): A well-formed formula that contains no free variables.

A formula with free variables (an open formula) cannot be evaluated as true or false on its own because the identity of the unquantified entity is unspecified. Only a sentence possesses a determinate truth value under a given domain interpretation.

1.7.5 Pitfalls
  • Functions vs. Predicates: A predicate produces a truth value () and can serve as a standalone condition or formula. A function returns an object in and can only appear as an argument inside a predicate, function, or equality assertion. Writing is an illegal syntax error because is a term, not a truth-bearing formula.
  • Treating Open Formulas as Sentences: cannot be assigned a truth value until is either bound by another quantifier (e.g., ) or substituted with a concrete constant (e.g., ).
1.8 Quantification, Negation, and Natural Language Translation in FOL

Quantification specifies the quantity of specimens in the domain of discourse that satisfy an open formula. First-order logic uses two primary quantifiers:

  • The universal quantifier (), read as “for all” or “for every”, asserts that a property holds for every individual in : Over a finite domain , universal quantification is semantically equivalent to an iterated conjunction:
  • The existential quantifier (), read as “there exists” or “for at least one”, asserts that a property holds for one or more individuals in : Over a finite domain , existential quantification behaves as an iterated disjunction:

Why it matters: Real-world knowledge representation requires stating general laws (e.g., integrity constraints, physical laws) and existence claims (e.g., finding an unassigned resource) across vast or infinite domains without explicitly enumerating every individual instance.

1.8.1 Quantifier Duality and Negation Laws

Applying De Morgan’s laws to iterated conjunctions and disjunctions yields the quantifier negation duality laws:

Pushing a negation through a quantifier flips the quantifier type () and negates the downstream subformula:

  • Negating “Every student passed” () yields “At least one student did not pass”:
  • Negating “Some student passed” () yields “No student passed” (i.e., every student failed):
1.8.2 Quantifier Ordering and Scope Alternation

When quantifiers of the same type appear consecutively, their order can be swapped without altering truth conditions: and .

However, when quantifiers of different types alternate, order is strictly sensitive to scope: 1. (“Everyone likes someone”): For each person , there is a person (possibly a different person for each ) such that likes . The choice of can depend functionally on . 2. (“There is someone whom everyone likes”): There exists a single, fixed individual such that every person in the domain likes that same .

The second statement is strictly stronger than the first: , but the converse does not hold.

1.8.3 Canonical Translation Patterns and Pitfalls

Natural language sentences map into first-order logic following standard syntactic pairings between quantifiers and connectives:

  • Universal statements map to material implication: “Every student takes Introduction to AI”: Common Pitfall: Using conjunction instead of implication. The formula asserts that every entity in the universe is simultaneously a student and enrolled in Introduction to AI (false if even one chair, course, or non-student exists in the domain).
  • Existential statements map to conjunction: “Some student takes Introduction to AI”: Common Pitfall: Using implication instead of conjunction. The formula evaluates to true whenever there is an object in the domain for which is false (since is vacuously true). If a pencil exists in the domain, the formula is satisfied regardless of whether any student takes the course.
1.8.4 Complex Relational Translations and Exact Quantification

Expressing multi-variable relations, nested restrictions, and numerical bounds requires structured scoping and equality constraints:

  • Multi-variable relational constraints:
    “All countries that border Ecuador are in South America”:
  • Nested quantifier scope comparison:
    • “Every student takes at least one course”:
    • “There is a course that every student takes”:
    • “There is a course that no student takes”:
    • “No student has passed every course”:
  • Exact quantification (Uniqueness):
    Standard logic lacks a dedicated “exactly ” symbol; it is formulated using equality (). “Exactly one student takes Introduction to AI” is expressed as the conjunction of existence (at least one) and uniqueness (at most one): Any object satisfying the same condition must be identical to .

2. Definitions

  • Epistemology: The philosophical study of the nature, origins, and limits of knowledge, investigating how justified true belief differs from mere opinion or guess.
  • Justified True Belief (JTB): The classical tripartite definition of knowledge asserting that an agent knows a proposition if and only if the proposition is true, the agent believes it, and the agent holds adequate justification for that belief.
  • Gettier Case: A counterexample showing that an agent can possess a justified true belief purely by coincidence, demonstrating that classical JTB is insufficient without a proper explanatory connection between justification and truth.
  • Turing Test: An operational benchmark for machine intelligence proposed by Alan Turing where a machine passes if a human interrogator communicating via text cannot distinguish its responses from those of an actual human.
  • CAPTCHA: A completely automated reverse Turing test that presents automated sensory or recognition challenges easily solved by humans but difficult for software to distinguish users from bots.
  • Chinese Room Argument: A thought experiment by John Searle demonstrating that executing formal, syntactic rule-based instructions does not produce intentionality, consciousness, or semantic understanding.
  • Syntax: The formal system of structural and grammatical rules governing the manipulation and combination of symbols without regard to their meanings.
  • Semantics: The meaning, real-world reference, and truth values associated with expressions and symbols.
  • Three Laws of Robotics: Isaac Asimov’s hierarchical ethical principles requiring a robot to avoid harming humans (Law 1), obey human orders unless conflicting with the first law (Law 2), and protect its own existence unless conflicting with the higher laws (Law 3).
  • Zeroth Law of Robotics: An overarching meta-rule stating that a robot must not injure humanity as a whole or allow humanity to come to harm through inaction, superseding duties to individual humans.
  • Proposition: A declarative statement that is definitively either true or false in classical logic, but cannot be both.
  • Compound Formula: A complex logical proposition formed by joining simpler propositions using logical operators.
  • Logical Operator: A functional connective—such as negation (), conjunction (), disjunction (), conditional (), or biconditional ()—that determines the truth value of a formula from the truth values of its component propositions.
  • Contrapositive: An equivalent formulation of an implication formed by negating and swapping both components, stating that is logically identical to .
  • Tautology: A propositional formula that evaluates to true under every possible assignment of truth values to its propositional variables.
  • Contradiction: A propositional formula that evaluates to false under every possible assignment of truth values to its propositional variables.
  • Contingency: A propositional formula that evaluates to true under at least one truth assignment and false under at least one other.
  • Satisfiable Formula: A logical expression for which there exists at least one truth assignment that makes the overall statement true.
  • Logical Equivalence: The relationship between two formulas indicating that they yield the exact same truth value under every possible interpretation or variable assignment.
  • First-Order Logic: A formal system that extends propositional logic by decomposing statements into domain objects, properties and relations via predicates, functions, and quantifiers.
  • Term: A syntactic expression in first-order logic—such as a constant, variable, or function evaluated on inputs—that designates an individual object within the domain.
  • Predicate: A logical symbol denoting a property or relation that maps one or more domain terms to a truth value.
  • Atomic Formula: The simplest well-formed formula in first-order logic consisting solely of a predicate applied to terms or an equality between two terms.
  • Universal Quantifier: The logical symbol indicating that a given predicate formula holds true for every object in the domain of discourse.
  • Existential Quantifier: The logical symbol indicating that a given predicate formula holds true for at least one object in the domain of discourse.
  • Free Variable: A variable occurring within a logical formula that is not bound by any universal or existential quantifier.
  • Bound Variable: A variable occurring within the scope of a quantifier that binds it.
  • Sentence (First-Order Logic): A well-formed first-order formula containing no free variables, allowing it to have a definite, evaluable truth value under a given interpretation.
